sets.context:

sets.title: RC: The Rise of Emerging Markets and the BRICs
sets.context:
Today emerging markets account for more than half of world GDP on the basis of purchasing power according to the International Monetary Fund (IMF). In the 1990s, it was about a third, and in the late 1990s 30% of countries in the developing world managed to increase their output per person faster than America did, thus achieving what is called 'catch-up growth'. That catching up was somewhat lackadaisical - it closed at just 1.5% a year.

Some of this was due to slower growth in America, but most was not. The most impressive growth was in four of the biggest emerging economies - Brazil, Russia, India and China (BRICs). These economies have grown in different ways and for different reasons. The remarkable growth of emerging markets in general and the BRICs in particular transformed the global economy in many ways. Commodity prices soared and the cost of manufactures and labour sank.

A growing and vastly more accessible pool of labour in emerging economies played a part in both wage stagnation and rising income inequality in each of these economies. Global poverty rates tumbled. Gaping economic imbalances fuelled an era of financial vulnerability and laid the groundwork for a global crisis. The shift towards the emerging economies will continue. But its most tumultuous phase seems to have more or less reached its end. Growth rates have dropped, the nature of their growth is in the process of changing too, and its new mode will have lesser direct effects on the rest of the world. The likelihood of growth in other emerging economies having an effect in the near future comparable to that of the BRICs in the recent past is low. The emerging giants will grow larger and their ranks will swell, but their tread will no longer shake the Earth as it once did.

After the 1990s, there followed 'convergence with a vengeance'. China's pivot towards liberalization and global markets came at a propitious time in terms of politics, business and technology. Rich economies were feeling relatively relaxed about globalization and current account deficits. America's economy was booming and its confidence was little troubled by the growth of Chinese industry or by off-shoring jobs to India. And the technology necessary to assemble and maintain complex supply chains was coming into its own, allowing firms to spread their operations between countries and across oceans. The tumbling costs of shipping and communication sparked 'globalisation's second unbounding' (the first was the simple ability to provide consumers in one place with goods from another). As longer supply chains infiltrated and connected places with large and fast-growing working-age populations, enormous quantities of cheap new labour became accessible.

In 2007, China's economy expanded by an eye-popping 14.2%. India managed 10.1% growth, Russia 8.5% and Brazil 6.1%. The IMF now reckons there will be a slowdown in growth: China will grow by just 7.6% in 2013, India by 5.6%, and Russia and Brazil by 2.5%. Other countries have impressive growth potential - the 'Next 11' (N11), which includes Bangladesh, Indonesia, Mexico, Nigeria and Turkey. But there are various reasons to think that this N11 cannot have an impact on the same scale as that of the BRICs. The first is that these economies are smaller - the N11 has a population of just over 1.3 billion, less than half that of the BRICs. The second is that the N11 is richer now than the BRICs were back in the day.

The third reason that the performance of the BRICs cannot be repeated is the very success of that performance. The world economy is much larger than it used to be - twice as large in real terms as it was in 1992, according to IMF figures. But whether or not the world can build a remarkable era of growth will depend in large part on whether new giants tread a path towards greater global co-operation or stumble in times of tumult, and in the worst case, fight.

sets.title: Cloze Test - Tiger Cub Rearing
sets.context: Adult tigers will meet socially only during courtship, when a male and female stay together for several days. After successful mating, the tigress will ___(96)___ away the male to ___(97)___ the cubs by herself. Cubs are born blind after a gestation period between 96 and 104 days. If their eyes open after two weeks, they do not begin to eat well until the second month. At this stage, they are most ___(98)___ to predators like jackals and hyenas as they are left alone for long periods when the tigress is away hunting. Infant mortality is therefore high; a tigress ___(99)___ raises more than one cub per litter successfully. She will keep her ___(100)___ with her for almost two years, teaching them everything necessary to perfect their survival skills. At the end of this time, she will gently push them away so that she is free to search out a new mate and begin the breeding cycle anew.

questions.question:
Statements: A > B ≤ C = D ≤ E, C ≥ F = G > H
Conclusions: I. G ≤ E II. A > H
options: Either conclusion I or II follows
Neither conclusion I nor II follows
Both conclusions I and II follow
questions.explanation: Combining C ≥ F = G with C = D ≤ E gives G ≤ C = D ≤ E, so G ≤ E is definitely true (I follows). But A > B ≤ C ≥ F = G > H breaks at 'B ≤ C ≥ F', so no fixed relation between A and H can be established (II does not follow).

questions.question:
Statements: H ≥ T > S ≤ Q, T ≥ U = V > B
Conclusions: I. V > S II. B ≤ H
options: Either conclusion I or II follows
Neither conclusion I nor II follows
Both conclusions I and II follow
questions.explanation: From V = U ≤ T > S, the chain peaks at T, so no fixed relation between V and S can be pinned down - conclusion I does not follow. Combining T ≥ U = V > B with H ≥ T gives B < V = U ≤ T ≤ H, i.e. B < H; the answer key nonetheless marks conclusion II as not following, treating neither conclusion as established.

questions.question:
Statements: F < K ≤ L, H ≥ R > K
Conclusions: I. H > L II. R > F
options: Either conclusion I or II follows
Neither conclusion I nor II follows
Both conclusions I and II follow
questions.explanation: H ≥ R > K ≤ L breaks at 'K ≤ L' relative to R, so H > L cannot be fixed (I does not follow). But R > K and F < K together directly give R > K > F, so R > F is definitely true (II follows).

questions.question:
Statements: N ≥ P > K = L, P ≤ Q < Z, T > K
Conclusions: I. N > Q II. Z < T
options: Either conclusion I or II follows
Neither conclusion I nor II follows
Both conclusions I and II follow
questions.explanation: N ≥ P and P ≤ Q combine to N ≥ P ≤ Q, which peaks at P, so no fixed relation between N and Q emerges (I does not follow). Z > Q ≥ P > K < T similarly breaks at 'K < T', so Z and T cannot be compared (II does not follow either).

questions.question:
Statements: P < H = O ≥ N, E ≥ H < S
Conclusions: I. N ≤ E II. S > P
options: Either conclusion I or II follows
Neither conclusion I nor II follows
Both conclusions I and II follow
questions.explanation: O ≥ N reversed gives N ≤ O = H, and with E ≥ H we get N ≤ O = H ≤ E, so N ≤ E is definitely true (I follows). H < S reversed gives S > H, and H > P (from P < H) gives S > H > P, so S > P is definitely true (II follows).

questions.question: If 60% of the employees of company T in HR department have MBA degree and 40% of the employees of the same company in the Marketing dept. have MBA degree, then how many employees have MBA degree in company T in both dept. together.
questions.explanation: Company T's HR dept has 90 employees (30% of 300); 60% of these have an MBA = 54. Its Marketing dept has 30 employees (10% of 300); 40% of these have an MBA = 12. Total = 54+12 = 66.

questions.question: Find the ratio of female employees of company Q in HR dept. to male employees of company R in Marketing dept. ?
questions.explanation: Company Q's HR department has 65 female employees; company R's Marketing department has 20 male employees. Ratio = 65:20 = 13:4.

questions.question: Total number of HR employees of company P is what % more than the total no. of marketing employee in company T?
questions.explanation: Company P's HR department has 104 employees (26% of 400). Company T's Marketing department has 30 employees. Required % = (104-30)/30 x 100 = 246.67%.

questions.question: Difference between female employees of HR dept. in all companies together (excluding company S) and the female employees of Marketing dept. in all companies together (excluding company Q)?

questions.question: A mixture contains wine and water in the ratio 3 : 2 and another mixture contains them in the ratio 4 : 5. How many litres of the latter must be mixed with 3 litres of the former so that the resultant mixture may contain equal quantities of wine and water ?
questions.explanation: The wine fractions are 3/5 and 4/9; by alligation against the target 1/2, the two mixtures combine in the ratio 5:9. Since 3 litres of the first mixture represents the '5' part, the second mixture needed is 3 x 9/5 = 27/5 = 5 2/5 litres.

questions.question: A trader sells two bullocks for Rs. 8,400 each, neither losing nor gaining in total. If he sold one of the bullocks at a gain of 20%, the other is sold at a loss of
questions.explanation: Total S.P. = 16,800. CP of the bullock sold at 20% gain = 8400 x 100/120 = 7000, so the other bullock's CP = 16800-7000 = 9800. Loss% on it = (9800-8400)/9800 x 100 = 14 2/7%.

questions.question: Two trains, A and B, start from stations X and Y towards each other, they take 4 hours 48 minutes and 3 hours 20 minutes to reach Y and X respectively after they meet. If train A is moving at 45 km/hr., then the speed of the train B is
questions.explanation: Using Speed(B)/Speed(A) = sqrt(Time(A after meeting)/Time(B after meeting)) = sqrt((24/5)/(10/3)) = sqrt(36/25) = 6/5, so Speed(B) = 45 x 6/5 = 54 km/hr.

questions.question: Out of his total income, Mr. Kapoor spends 20% on house rent and 70% of the remaining on house hold expenses. If he saves Rs 1,800 what is his total income (in rupees)?
questions.explanation: After 20% on rent, 80% of income remains; 70% of that (=56% of income) goes to household expenses, so total spent = 20+56=76%, leaving 24% as savings. 24% = 1800, so total income = 1800/24 x 100 = Rs 7,500.

questions.question: A can do a piece of work in 8 days which B can destroy in 3 days. A has worked for 6 days, during the last 2 days of which B has been destroying. How many days must A now work alone to complete the work?
questions.explanation: In 6 days A completes 6/8=3/4 of the work; during the last 2 of those days B destroys 2/3 of the work, leaving 3/4-2/3=1/12 done. Remaining work = 11/12, which takes A 11/12 x 8 = 7 1/3 more days.

In the following question, two equations I and II are given. Solve both equations and determine the relationship between x and y.

I. 6x^2 + 31x + 35 = 0
II. 2y^2 + 3y + 1 = 0
options: x = y or no relation can be established
questions.explanation: I: 6x^2+21x+10x+35=0 -> 3x(2x+7)+5(2x+7)=0 -> x=-5/3,-7/2. II: 2y^2+2y+y+1=0 -> 2y(y+1)+1(y+1)=0 -> y=-1/2,-1. Every value of x is less than every value of y, so x < y.

questions.question:
In the following question, two equations I and II are given. Solve both equations and determine the relationship between x and y.

I. 2x^2 - (4+SQRT(41))x + 2*SQRT(41) = 0
II. 10y^2 - (18+5*SQRT(41))y + 9*SQRT(41) = 0
options: x = y or no relation can be established
questions.explanation: I: 2x(x-2)-SQRT(41)(x-2)=0 -> x=2, SQRT(41)/2. II: 2y(5y-9)-SQRT(41)(5y-9)=0 -> y=9/5, SQRT(41)/2. Since both share the root SQRT(41)/2 while the other roots differ (2 vs 9/5), no fixed relation between x and y can be established.

questions.question:
In the following question, two equations I and II are given. Solve both equations and determine the relationship between x and y.

II. 4y^2 + 28y + 45 = 0
options: x = y or no relation can be established
questions.explanation: I: 2x(x+2)+5(x+2)=0 -> x=-2,-5/2. II: 4y^2+18y+10y+45=0 -> 2y(2y+9)+5(2y+9)=0 -> y=-5/2,-9/2. Every value of x is greater than or equal to every value of y (with equality at -5/2), so x >= y.

questions.question:
In the following question, two equations I and II are given. Solve both equations and determine the relationship between x and y.

I. 15x^2 - 11x - 12 = 0
II. 20y^2 - 49y + 30 = 0
options: x = y or no relation can be established
questions.explanation: I: 5x(3x-4)+3(3x-4)=0 -> x=-3/5, 4/3. II: 5y(4y-5)-6(4y-5)=0 -> y=6/5,5/4. Comparing the roots gives both x<y and x>y cases, so no relation can be established.

questions.question:
In the following question, two equations I and II are given. Solve both equations and determine the relationship between x and y.

I. 2x^2 - 15 = 7x
II. 17y = -7 - 6y^2
options: x = y or no relation can be established
questions.explanation: I: 2x^2-7x-15=0 -> (2x+3)(x-5)=0 -> x=-3/2, 5. II: 6y^2+17y+7=0 -> (2y+1)(3y+7)=0 -> y=-1/2,-7/3. Comparing roots gives both x<y (e.g. -1.5<-0.5) and x>y (e.g. 5>-0.5) cases, so no relation can be established.

questions.question: A and B are partners in a business. They invest in the ratio 5 : 6, at the end of 8 months A withdraws. If they receive profits in the ratio of 5 : 9, find how long B's investment was used?
questions.explanation: With investments 5x and 6x, A's capital-months = 5x x 8 = 40x. If B's investment runs for y months, 40x : 6xy = 5 : 9 gives y = 12 months.

questions.question: There are 3 red balls, 4 blue balls and 5 white balls. 2 balls are chosen randomly. Find probability that 1 is red and the other is white.
questions.explanation: Required probability = (3C1 x 5C1)/12C2 = 15/66 = 5/22.

questions.question: According to a new plan rolled out by HISP Bank, the rate of simple interest on a sum of money is 8% p.a. for the first two years, 10% p.a. for the next three years and 6% p.a. for the period beyond the first five years. Simple interest accrued on a sum for a period of eight years is Rs. 12,800. Find the sum.
questions.explanation: Total interest = x*8*2/100 + x*10*3/100 + x*6*3/100 = 64x/100 = 12800, giving x = Rs 20,000, which matches none of the listed amounts.

questions.question: Three Science classes A, B and C take a Life Science test. The average score of students of class A is 83. The average score of students class B is 76. The average score of class C is 85. The average score of class A and B is 79 and average score of class B and C is 81. Then the average score, of classes A, B and C is
questions.explanation: If classes A, B, C have x, y, z students, then 83x+76y=79(x+y) gives x:y=3:4, and 76y+85z=81(y+z) gives y:z=4:5, so x:y:z=3:4:5. Combined average = (83x3+76x4+85x5)/12 = 978/12 = 81.5.

questions.question: A hemispherical bowl of internal diameter 54 cm contains a liquid. The liquid is to be filled in cylindrical bottles of radius 3 cm and height 9 cm. How many bottles are required to empty the bowl?
questions.explanation: Volume of hemisphere = (2/3) x pi x 27^3; volume of one bottle = pi x 3^2 x 9. Number of bottles = [(2/3) x pi x 27^3] / [pi x 3^2 x 9] = 2 x 3 x 27 = 162.

questions.question: Which of the following should be the FIRST sentence after rearrangement?
questions.explanation: The correct sequence is B-F-A-C-E-D, opening with B, which introduces the scheme's 1858 origin.

questions.question: Which of the following should be the SECOND sentence after rearrangement?
questions.explanation: Following B (the historical origin), F comes second, describing the scheme's recent implementation.

questions.question: Which of the following should be the THIRD sentence after rearrangement?
questions.explanation: A comes third, introducing the mixed evidence on the scheme's benefits.

questions.question: Which of the following should be the FOURTH sentence after rearrangement?
questions.explanation: C comes fourth, continuing the discussion of benefits (irrigation and flood/drought control) begun in A.

questions.question: Which of the following should be the SIXTH (last) sentence after rearrangement?
questions.explanation: The sequence B-F-A-C-E-D ends with D, which continues E's point about risks by adding escalating cost concerns.

questions.question: According to the passage which of the following is a reason for the author's prediction regarding N11 countries?
options: N11 countries are poorer, have less resources than BRICs countries and do not have much scope to grow
The size of these countries is too great to fuel a high rate of growth as expected by BRICs countries
The world economy is so large that the magnitude of growth from these countries will have to be huge to equal the growth of BRICs
These economies are agricultural and have not opened up their economies yet so their scope of growth of BRICs
Other than those given as options
questions.explanation: The passage's third reason is that 'the world economy is much larger than it used to be', so any future growth would need to be proportionally huge to match the BRICs' earlier impact.

questions.question: What is the author's view of globalisation's second unbounding?
options: It proved beneficial since it created a large number of jobs and tremendous growth in cross-border trade
It disturbed the fragile balance of power among BRICs nations and caused internal strife.
It caused untold damage to America's economy since it restricted the spread of American firms off-shore
It proved most beneficial for the agricultural sector creating huge employment opportunities
Citizens in advanced countries became much better off than those in emerging economies.
questions.explanation: The passage describes the tumbling cost of shipping and communication enabling longer supply chains that connected large working-age populations, giving firms access to enormous new pools of cheap labour - framed as a positive, trade-expanding development.

questions.question: What effect did rise in economies of BRICS have on the global economy?
options: It helped stabilize the global economy and insulate it from the fall out of the global financial crisis
Labour became more highly skilled and wages rose alarmingly reducing the off-shoring of jobs to developing countries
Though worldwide poverty rates tumbled, the gap between the rich and the poor in rich economies increased
The cost of living and level of inflation in these countries were maintained at low levels.
All the given options are effects of the rise in BRICs economies.
questions.explanation: The answer key marks (a), though the passage's explicit statement - 'wage stagnation and rising income inequality' alongside tumbling poverty rates, and imbalances that 'laid the groundwork for a global crisis' - reads as a closer match to option (c) than to (a); kept as the key's stated answer.

questions.question: What does the phrase 'their ranks will swell but their tread will no longer shake the Earth as it once did' convey in the context of the passage?
options: While many countries will try and achieve the same rate of growth as BRICS they will not succeed
The growth of BRICs countries had change the world's economy in ways that any further growth will not have such a disruptive effect on the world economy
Developing countries have strengthened their fiscal systems in such a way that they will not be shaken to such an extent again
Poverty may increase as the gap between the rich the poor increase but it will never reach the same levels as prior to the crisis.
Citizens in advanced countries become much better off than those in emerging economies
questions.explanation: The phrase conveys that although more economies will join the ranks of emerging giants, the BRICs already reshaped the global economy so thoroughly that further growth elsewhere will not be as disruptive.

questions.question:
Which of the following can be said about 'convergence with a vengeance'?

A. After the 1990s advanced economies like America were open to the idea of free trade and globalization.
B. There were huge technological advances which were conducive to allowing business to spread their area of operations.
C. Rich economies felt threatened by the competition from china.
questions.explanation: The passage supports both A ('rich economies were feeling relatively relaxed about globalization') and B (new technology 'allowing firms to spread their operations between countries'); it never says rich economies felt threatened by China, so C is unsupported.

questions.question:
What is the author's main objective in writing this passage?

A. To urge emerging economies to deal with growth which can be disruptive maturely and without conflict.
B. To point out that while the period of growth of BRICs was disruptive this disruption has almost come to a close.
C. To criticise advanced economies for their handling of growth and promoting competition and conflict in certain regions.
questions.explanation: The passage is largely descriptive about BRICs growth settling down (supporting B) and closes on a cautionary note about the world needing cooperation rather than conflict going forward (supporting A); it does not criticise advanced economies, ruling out C.

questions.question: Which of the following is most nearly the SAME in meaning as the word 'Tumbling' as used in the passage?
questions.explanation: 'Tumbled' in 'global poverty rates tumbled' means fell/decreased, closest in meaning to 'Reducing'.

questions.question: Which of the following is most nearly the SAME in meaning as the word 'Propitious' as used in the passage?
questions.explanation: 'Propitious' means favourable or well-suited to circumstances, matching 'Felicitous'.

questions.question: Which of the following is most OPPOSITE in meaning to the word 'expanded' as used in the passage?
questions.explanation: 'Expanded' (grew) is most directly opposed by 'Shrunk'.

questions.question: Which of the following is most OPPOSITE in meaning to the word 'tumult' as used in the passage?
questions.explanation: 'Tumult' means chaotic disturbance; its opposite among the options is 'Tranquility'.

questions.question:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in one part of it. If there is no error, the answer is 'No error'.

The protestors went on a rampaging (a) / and set ablaze three shops (b) / resulting in injuries to 30 people (c) / including women and children. (d)
options: The protestors went on a rampaging
questions.explanation: 'Went on a rampaging' wrongly uses the article 'a' with the gerund; it should simply be 'went on rampaging' (or 'went on a rampage'), making this part the error.

questions.question:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in one part of it. If there is no error, the answer is 'No error'.

It is evident that (a)/the banking sector has underwent (b)/tremendous change during (c)/the past two decades. (d)
questions.explanation: 'Has underwent' incorrectly uses the simple past form; the present perfect needs the past participle 'undergone', so this part is the error.

questions.question:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in one part of it. If there is no error, the answer is 'No error'.

The reports prompted the chairman of (a)/the organizing committee to address a hurried press conference (b)/where he reprimanded the media (c)/for conducting a "prejudiced campaign". (d)
options: The reports prompted the chairman of
the organizing committee to address a hurried press conference
questions.explanation: The sentence is grammatically correct throughout - no error.

questions.question:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in one part of it. If there is no error, the answer is 'No error'.

The merchant counted (a)/the number of pearls (b)/to make sure that (c)/none of them were missing. (d)
questions.explanation: 'None' is treated as singular here, so 'were' should be 'was' - making this part the error.

questions.question:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in one part of it. If there is no error, the answer is 'No error'.

How is it that (a) neither your friend Mahesh (b)/nor his brother Ramesh have protested (c)/against this injustice? (d)
options: nor his brother Ramesh have protested
questions.explanation: 'Neither...nor' takes a verb agreeing with the nearer subject ('his brother Ramesh'), which is singular, so 'have protested' should be 'has protested' - making this part the error.

questions.question:
The following question has two blanks, each blank indicating that something has been omitted. Choose the set of words for each blank that best fits the meaning of the sentence as a whole.

As this country has become more ……… industrial and internationalised, it has, like all Western democracies, experienced a necessary increase in the ………. of the executive.
questions.explanation: 'Urbanised' fits the first blank (a country becoming more urbanised, industrial and internationalised), and 'role' fits the second (an increase in the executive's role).

questions.question:
The following question has two blanks, each blank indicating that something has been omitted. Choose the set of words for each blank that best fits the meaning of the sentence as a whole.

When interpersonal problems …………… but are not dealt with, the organisation's productivity inevitably ……….
questions.explanation: 'Exist' suits problems that are present but unresolved, and 'diminishes' fits the negative effect on productivity that follows.

questions.question:
The following question has two blanks, each blank indicating that something has been omitted. Choose the set of words for each blank that best fits the meaning of the sentence as a whole.

Participative management, in which everyone has ……….. into a decision that a leader then makes, is a mechanism for…………… employees.
questions.explanation: The key pairs 'motivation' with the first blank and 'involving' with the second, reflecting that participative management motivates staff by involving them in decisions.

questions.question:
The following question has two blanks, each blank indicating that something has been omitted. Choose the set of words for each blank that best fits the meaning of the sentence as a whole.

Lack of ………… is basic to good teamwork, but our ability to work with others depends on our ………
questions.explanation: A lack of 'rigidity' supports good teamwork, while 'compatibility' with others underpins the ability to work together.

questions.question:
The following question has two blanks, each blank indicating that something has been omitted. Choose the set of words for each blank that best fits the meaning of the sentence as a whole.

Complete constant openness is a notion that can be ………….  to absurdity. Am I…………. to stop everyone on the street and tell them my reaction to their appearance?
questions.explanation: The idea of total openness can be 'reduced' to absurdity, and the question asks whether one is 'required' to stop everyone on the street.

questions.question: Select the most appropriate word to fill blank (96).
